items.title: Man on ‘Mission’ to Handwrite Entire New Testament: ‘Anchor for My Soul’
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "A starving man being invited into a banquet."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

It took Don Ashley about 210 hours over eight months and 15 days to write his own handwritten copy of the New Testament.

Ashley, a recently retired university administrator who relocated from Anchorage, Alaska, to farmland in Arkansas, posted to social media this month that he’d just completed the project — an endeavor he said he began “on a whim” on Jan. 5.

View on Threads

But what started as an impulse quickly turned into what he called “a mission.”

“In all these life transitions,” he told CBN News, “this really served as an anchor for my soul.”

The idea, he explained, was born out of a work trip to the Society of Biblical Literature, a 146-year-old learning society dedicated to the academic study of the Bible and other ancient writings.

When he was at the meeting in San Diego, Ashley saw a display of the Dead Sea Scrolls, a collection of roughly 1,000 ancient Jewish manuscripts dating from the 3rd century B.C. to the 1st century A.D. They were discovered in the 1940s and 50s.

“I was so impressed by the artistry required … that I wanted to experience something about what the ancient scribes experienced,” Ashley said.

The average American spends about two-and-a-half hours per day on social media. For teenagers, that number is nearly doubled, spending roughly five hours every day on social media apps. And 41% of teens who reported the highest social media use rated their mental health as poor or very poor, according to data from the American Psychological Association.

Much of that time is spent doomscrolling, a term that first broke into the American lexicon through Twitter in 2018 and was officially added to the dictionary in late 2020. The concept became pretty commonplace at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, when Americans of all ages were stuck at home spending an outsized portion of their days scrolling content on their phones.

Doomscrolling, for the uninitiated, is the habit of spending excessive time online browsing through often negative, depressing, and alarming news content. Needless to say, dedicating a great deal of energy to that kind of content can quickly become distressing and take a significant toll on users’ mental health — particularly if they have no belief in a sovereign God who promises to work together all things to the good of those who love Him (Romans 8:28).

As for Ashley, he felt handwriting the Bible was a better, more profitable use of his time.

“I think the idea that, instead of doomscrolling, maybe you could do something more useful with your time,” he said. “The world is so fast-paced now, maybe it appeals to the idea of slowing down.”

The process was deeply cathartic for Ashley, who is currently recovering from a significant back surgery. He likened the project, in a spiritual sense, to “a starving man being invited into a banquet.”

“I made mistakes on this page and I didn’t worry too much about the mistakes,” he said, holding up a page from his journal where he’d marked over some errors. “I just lined through them and kept going.”

When it was all said and done, Ashley noted that — while he didn’t walk away with any new theological revelations — it was spiritually encouraging to physically experience Scripture in a new way.

“I’ve experienced the Bible with my mind for my whole career and since my initial conversion experience in 1985,” he said, “but I wanted to experience it with my fingers. Putting a pen to paper is a different experience than reading it.”

items.title: First Liberty: Minnesota County Has ‘Essentially Criminalized Being Amish’
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

The Amish community in Minnesota is pushing back amid claims of unfair government policies that purportedly fail to offer religious accommodations — and even reportedly led to one Amish man’s arrest.

First Liberty attorney Ryan Gardner said his firm is representing two Amish congregations in Mille Lacs County, Minnesota, arguing the county itself has “essentially criminalized being Amish.”

“As you might know, the Amish community lives by a pretty strict set of religious principles, and many of those involve not being involved in technology,” Gardner said. “And kind of keeping to themselves … they want to be able to live according to their religious beliefs, and a lot of what those beliefs require, frankly … to be set apart from modern society.”

According to First Liberty, problems began for these congregations during COVID-19, when county officials reportedly implemented a new permitting system for building structures and homes.

“It went from a paper form to an electronic form,” Gardner said. “As you might imagine, the Amish don’t really use electronic forms or the internet, so this was a significant problem, and they had no alternative for a long time.”

With no other option for simply getting clearance to build homes, he said “a lot of the people in these congregations just proceeded to build anyways because they didn’t have a choice.”

Gardner said Mille Lacs County did eventually change the policy to make a paper option available, but added there is an additional $50 fee for requesting permitting on paper.

“Pretty much the only people who are actually using that are the Amish, and so now they’re having to pay a special fee just to even start the permitting process,” the lawyer said. “And once they get in, there are more problems because they’re trying to impose all kinds of modern requirements that are just inconsistent with the Amish way of life.”

Gardner said officials have been so hard on the Amish that they even put one man in jail “for the crime of building and living in his home.”

“This particular individual had been living in his home for something like five years and then, suddenly, he’s criminally cited for it, and he goes to court, and he’s convicted,” the lawyer said. “And he is … immediately taken to jail.”

Gardner said it is “ludicrous” and “extreme” to prosecute someone for such a “petty” offense, and added that such a reaction is rare. He added that the Amish had purportedly tried to go to the county to work the issue out but were “met with hostility.”

“Here’s the kicker in all of this,” he continued, “Built into the very ordinance that the county is enforcing here is a provision that gives the county discretion to give exemptions to these requirements to anybody that it wants.”

First Liberty sent a letter to the county recently demanding they stop enforcement actions against the Amish, especially considering warrants that are currently out for others. They’re also looking for an exemption that would settle the issue once and for all, noting that, from his perspective, the Amish build insanely safe structures.

Mille Lacs County told CBN News that lawyers cannot comment on ongoing cases.

items.title: A Christian Dating App Just Added a ‘Chivalry Mode’
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Most dating apps are built around keeping things casual. Upward, a Christian dating app, just relaunched around the opposite idea, and it gave that idea a setting. It’s called Chivalry Mode. When both people opt in, he’s encouraged to send the first message, and she decides whether to re
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Most dating apps are built around keeping things casual. Upward, a Christian dating app, just relaunched around the opposite idea, and it gave that idea a setting.

It’s called Chivalry Mode. When both people opt in, he’s encouraged to send the first message, and she decides whether to respond or “politely unmatch.”

The feature is part of a relaunch Upward announced Tuesday, repositioning the app as “the home of modern courtship.” It also added a Marriage Timeline, where members share when they hope to get married and can see whether a match is on a similar schedule, and a Core Values section that puts priorities on a profile up front.

Upward launched in 2020 as an app for Christian singles and is owned by Match Group, the company behind Tinder and Hinge. The relaunch is aimed at a wider crowd. Match’s own Singles in America research found 72 percent of Gen Z want to get married, more than any other generation, and the company says about one in four U.S. singles ages 18 to 34 strongly identify with traditional values around family, faith and community.

The company is fairly direct about the pitch.

“For a generation told to keep things casual and see where they go, saying you want marriage can almost feel countercultural,” said Lauren DeFord, Match Group’s director of brand marketing.

According to Upward, nearly every member ages 18 to 30 it surveyed says they want a family, which makes “family” the most-selected value on the app. And the No. 1 reason members say they leave is that they found someone worth leaving for.

Chivalry, it turns out, now has a toggle.

items.title: A Conversation with Bonnie Engstrom, Mother of Fulton Sheen’s ‘Miracle Baby’
items.author: Word on Fire
items.summary:
Word on Fire

“He was without a heartbeat for sixty-one minutes—a little over an hour. I believe with my whole heart that Fulton Sheen was walking with us and making a Holy Hour.”
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Word on Fire

The following is a conversation between Mytae Carrasco Wallace, the leader of the Word on Fire Institute’s Prayer Community, and Bonnie Engstrom, the mother of James Fulton Engstrom, the recipient of the miraculous healing through the intercession of Archbishop Fulton Sheen. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. 

* * *

Mytae Carrasco Wallace: Bonnie, we are so excited to have you here. So many Catholics have heard of Archbishop Fulton Sheen but may not really know or have an awareness of what led to his beatification. Would you kindly share how your family has played a role in these events?

Bonnie Engstrom: Yes. My son James Fulton is the recipient of the miracle that was approved by the Vatican and Pope Francis in 2019 that has allowed for Fulton Sheen to be beatified this September. 

James is my third son, and we had a planned home birth. He was born at home with medical care present. Everything about my pregnancy and the labor were totally normal, healthy, and beautiful, but there was a knot in James’s umbilical cord. We did not know it was present. And during the delivery, the knot tightened. It tightened so much that it cut off his oxygen supply so when James was delivered, he was a stillborn.

There in our bedroom, they immediately began CPR and called 911. In the middle of that, I remember sitting on my bedroom floor and watching my midwife do chest compressions on James. And I remember thinking in my head, “Fulton Sheen, Fulton Sheen, Fulton Sheen . . .” because I was in a state of shock. I was taking in what was happening, but I couldn’t process it. And I didn’t really know what to do, but I had this friendship with Fulton Sheen. In that moment, I was falling. I was just spiraling. I didn’t know what to do. And I called out Fulton Sheen’s name for him to catch me. 

In the ambulance, they did different things to try to restart his heart. He was hooked to a heart monitor and was pulseless. He did not have any kind of a heartbeat. Nothing worked that they tried. We got to the emergency room, again, they tried everything that they could to restart his heart. Nothing worked. And all hands came off so they could call the time of death. And it was at that moment—which was sixty-one minutes from the delivery to that moment—James’s heart came back to a full, strong, healthy heartbeat. It never stopped again.

He was without a heartbeat for sixty-one minutes—a little over an hour. I believe with my whole heart that Fulton Sheen was walking with us through it. I believe he was making a Holy Hour. From the day of his ordination, he made a promise to God that he would make a daily Holy Hour, and he kept that promise for over sixty years. When this Holy Hour was over, it was at that sixty-first minute that our Lord brought James back to life.

Immediately, it was all hands back on deck trying to stabilize him. They took him up to the NICU. There were seven weeks in the NICU, and there were lots of ups and downs. For James, they expected massive organ failure. So we took this in and processed it the best that we could—just hoping against hope, praying that God would perform a miracle, asking for Fulton Sheen’s intercession, and just trusting in the Lord’s goodness for whatever would happen. But it was definitely hard. As beautiful as it was, it was definitely hard.

When James was in the first twenty-four to thirty-six hours of his life, he had an MRI done. There were several imaging tests done, and those all showed that he had brain damage. And when he was three months old, we had a follow-up MRI done, and that showed a completely healthy brain.

Once we had the results of that follow-up MRI, it was actually my mom who said, “You need to contact the Sheen Foundation and let them know about this.” And I remember being like, “Mom, I know the sisters at the Sheen Foundation. People talk to them all the time about miracles. It doesn’t matter.” And she was like, “Bonnie, they’re going to want to put this in a file somewhere.”

So out of obedience to my mother, I called Sr. Anne at the Sheen Foundation and told her, and she was like, “This is amazing.” The word trickled on eventually to the bishop, and he talked to the postulator in Rome who was helping us with the cause. And he said, “We need to do an investigation.”

When James was a year old, there was an official tribunal that lasted three months. At the end of that, they interviewed doctors, nurses, basically anyone who could answer questions about if a miracle had happened. That was all sent to Rome where the postulator kind of compiled it and then submitted it to the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints. They have a team of medical advisors who study those cases, and the medical advisors actually asked for more information, so we took James to some follow-up physicals and things like that. More paperwork was sent over. And in the end, the medical advisors unanimously agreed that it was a medical miracle. 

Then it went to some theologians who were looking into whether it happened through Fulton Sheen’s intercession. They unanimously agreed that it did happen through Fulton Sheen’s intercession. And so then it went to the cardinals who make up that congregation, and they unanimously approved it as a miracle. 

In 2019, Pope Francis finally got to his desk, and he approved it as a miracle for Fulton Sheen’s beatification.

You said you were saying Fulton Sheen’s name throughout this shock, and you had already developed a friendship there. What inspired you and your husband to ask Fulton Sheen’s intercession throughout this pregnancy?

I was actually writing a grant. I was asking for money from a group that was named after Bishop Sheen. Because of that, I started watching videos of him on YouTube preaching and episodes of his old television show. And I was just so taken by him. I was a stay-at-home mom with two little kids, and I remember my husband coming home from work one day. I pulled him over to the computer, and I was like, “Look at him. He’s from our diocese. He grew up here. We can go and visit the place he was born and the place where he served Mass. It’s twenty minutes away from us.”

We were just so drawn to him, someone from the Midwest—just a little dot on the map that people fly over and don’t really care about. But here was this man who had done great things, who loved Jesus. And he was brilliant, and he was funny, and he was humble, and he was one of us.

We knew that his cause was open, and the Diocese of Peoria was working with the Vatican for his cause for canonization. So we just felt for sure that he was going to be pronounced a saint at one point in the future, and so we wanted to name our son after this future saint. It was during that pregnancy, because of Life is Worth Living and different homilies that he gave, that’s what really made us fall in love with him and want to put our son under his patronage to kind of invite him into our family. The saints, we invite them into our families and make them one of us.

That’s so true and such a testament to God’s love through the saints and the powerful witness the saints can give to us here on this earthly pilgrimage. They’re in it with us.

During those sixty-one minutes when your son’s heart stopped beating, how did you hope against hope? Here you are experiencing an agony similar to our Blessed Mother, walking in the sorrowful mysteries of your own life. How did you believe that? How did you continue to pray forward through that moment?

I honestly believed that I could not, and I had to rely on Fulton Sheen to do it for me. And part of that is because I was in that state of shock. I think I lived in a state of shock for weeks, honestly. I just had to trust in the Lord.

I had to hope in what I knew of the Lord, and I had to hope that Fulton Sheen and our Blessed Mother and others—St. Elizabeth is a patron of mine, and St. James the Greater is too. I had to hope that they were supporting me and carrying me with their prayers, and really, the whole body of the church. 

In the NICU, they try to give you hope. They offered something like, “James could be totally fine, or James could be dead by Friday.” They didn’t say it that bluntly, but we understood that they didn’t actually think James was going to be fine. But they thought James was going to be dead by Friday. Or if he wasn’t, he was going to have a very complicated life and a lot of suffering. 

We may be undergoing suffering or a trial that seems too much for us to bear—too great that it takes our breath away—but it’s like he literally carries us. He’s like, “I’m going to shield you. It’s happening, but for the parts of it that would cause you to panic, to run away, I’m going to hold you, and we’re going to go through it together.”

Have you or your family faced any challenges along the way being the spotlight and receiving this miracle? How has it grown your faith?

This is such a fun question. It has been such a privilege to be a part of this whole experience. From beginning to end, there have been opportunities to meet people and to go places, to speak and share our story, to write a book, and things like that I otherwise would not have had the ability or opportunity to do. So that has been really an amazing thing about the whole situation.
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

But it also has been kind of hard. And I feel silly saying that, but I think parenting James is what has been tough, because my husband and I feel very much like this is not our story. This is God’s story, and this happened to us for the good of the Church and the glory of God. So if we can share that, that is a beautiful thing. But God has also put us in charge of a unique soul and a very awesome kid, and we need to protect his privacy and give him a normal childhood. He’s a teenager now, and raising teenagers is different. They provide their own unique challenges. We try to make sure that we are doing a good job and doing what’s best for James in a way that honors the Lord as well. I think doing what’s best for James does honor the Lord because that’s our vocation. We put him first in his privacy and letting him enjoy it all as well. Sometimes it’s really fun to be the miracle baby, you know?

How has this relationship between Archbishop Fulton Sheen and James unfolded throughout the years?

He’s actually pretty private about his prayer life, but sometimes he will say things like, “I was praying, and I was asking Fulton Sheen to pray with me about da-da-da-da.” He has talked about how Fulton Sheen is still someone that he talks to every day, and he is a part of his faith and his spiritual journey, which I think is awesome. That is just so beautiful. A lot of that is on his own. He has been the one to maintain that and carry that banner, which is really cool.

As a very close friend to Archbishop Fulton Sheen on this side of heaven, how has sharing his impact on your family changed your own personal relationship with the Lord?

Bishop Sheen is well known for his devotion to the Blessed Mother and for his devotion to the Eucharist. He’s known for other things as well, of course, but his witness of those things have really changed my heart.

He has a book called The World’s First Love, and reading that just rocked my world. It blew my mind, and I have never looked at the Holy Family the same. So that was just a pivotal moment for me. I carry that with me every day. Every day when I walk with the Blessed Mother and I ask for her intercession—like Bishop Sheen has said and how he has informed me about her—it’s making a daily impact in my life.

On top of that, before my husband Travis and I even knew Bishop Sheen, we were Catholic because of the Eucharist, one hundred percent—huge devotion to our Lord and the Eucharist. But the more we look at Bishop Sheen’s witness—his daily Holy Hour and the way that he writes about the priesthood, the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass, and the importance of our Eucharistic Lord—all of those things have become foundational in our marriage and in the way that we’ve raised our kids. 

People talk about his conversions—and he led to a lot of conversions and some very influential conversions—but that was because he had personal connections and interactions one on one with people where he brought them back to the Lord because he was personally invested in them. They could see that he cared about them.

He won an Emmy, he had a television show, he had millions of viewers, but it was the personal one-on-one interactions and connections—that’s what mattered. And I think that’s been my biggest takeaway through this whole process, and a lesson that I had to learn was that the biggest impact comes from loving people who are right in front of me.

items.title: Thursday, September 24, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, we see Herod interested in and perplexed by Jesus.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Ecclesiastes 1:2-11

Vanity of vanities, says the Teacher,
    vanity of vanities! All is vanity.
What do people gain from all the toil
    at which they toil under the sun?
A generation goes, and a generation comes,
    but the earth remains forever.
The sun rises and the sun goes down,
    and hurries to the place where it rises.
The wind blows to the south,
    and goes around to the north;
round and round goes the wind,
    and on its circuits the wind returns.
All streams run to the sea,
    but the sea is not full;
to the place where the streams flow,
    there they continue to flow.
All things are wearisome;
    more than one can express;
the eye is not satisfied with seeing,
    or the ear filled with hearing.
What has been is what will be,
    and what has been done is what will be done;
    there is nothing new under the sun.
Is there a thing of which it is said,
    “See, this is new”?
It has already been,
    in the ages before us.
The people of long ago are not remembered,
    nor will there be any remembrance
of people yet to come
    by those who come after them.

Psalm
Psalm 90:3-4, 5-6, 12-13, 14, 17bc

You turn us back to dust,
    and say, “Turn back, you mortals.”
For a thousand years in your sight
    are like yesterday when it is past,
    or like a watch in the night.
You sweep them away; they are like a dream,
    like grass that is renewed in the morning;
in the morning it flourishes and is renewed;
    in the evening it fades and withers.
So teach us to count our days
    that we may gain a wise heart.
Turn, O Lord! How long?
    Have compassion on your servants!
Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love,
    so that we may rejoice and be glad all our days.
Let the favor of the Lord our God be upon us,
    and prosper for us the work of our hands—
    O prosper the work of our hands!

Gospel Reading
Luke 9:7-9

Now Herod the ruler heard about all that had taken place, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead, by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the ancient prophets had arisen. Herod said, “John I beheaded; but who is this about whom I hear such things?” And he tried to see him.

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, we see Herod interested in and perplexed by Jesus.

Political rulers don’t come across well in the New Testament. In Luke’s Christmas account, Caesar Augustus is compared very unfavorably to the Christ child. And in Matthew’s account, that child is hunted down by the desperate Herod. Later, Herod’s son persecutes John the Baptist and Jesus himself. More to it, the Jewish authorities are seen in all of the Gospels as corrupt.

And Pontius Pilate is a typical Roman governor: efficient, concerned for order, brutal. Like the other rulers of the time, he perceives Jesus, quite correctly, as a threat. “Then you are a king?” Pilate asks. Jesus says, “My kingdom does not belong to this world.”

This does not mean that Jesus is unconcerned for the realities of politics, with the very “this-worldly” concerns of justice, peace, and right order. When he speaks of his kingdom not belonging to the “world,” he shades the negative side of that term. The “world” is the realm of sin, selfishness, hatred, violence. What he is saying is that his way of ordering things is not typical of worldly powers like Pilate, Caesar, and Herod.
